sections.b: Isaiah's collection of oracles against the nations opens with Babylon (Isaiah 13:1–14:23) and returns to it in the riddle of 'the wilderness of the sea' (Isaiah 21:1–10). Chapter 13 pictures the LORD mustering an army from the edge of the sky, the Medes, to overturn Babylon like Sodom and Gomorrah and leave it to desert animals. Chapter 14 sets a taunt song in the mouths of freed Israelites: the king of Babylon goes down to Sheol, where the shades greet him, and 'Shining One, son of Dawn' falls from the heavens. Chapter 21 hears the cry 'Fallen! Fallen is Babylon!', which Revelation 14:8 and Revelation 18:2 take up for 'Babylon the Great'. Readers date these oracles either to the Assyrian period, when Babylon rebelled again and again (Merodach-baladan; Sennacherib's sack in 689 BC), or to the years before Cyrus took the city in 539 BC.
sections.refs: Isaiah 13:1–22; Isaiah 14:1–23; Isaiah 21:1–10; Isaiah 39:1–8; Revelation 14:8; Revelation 18:2

common: Most readers take Isaiah 13 and 21 to look ahead to the fall of Babylon to Cyrus and the Medes and Persians in 539 BC.
uncommon: Some scholars set both oracles in Isaiah's own century, when Assyria crushed Babylonian revolts in 710 and 689 BC.

sections.h: Assyria in Isaiah's oracles on the nations
sections.b: Though Babylon heads the collection, Assyria is the power behind most of Isaiah 13–23. A short oracle sworn by the LORD of Armies promises to break Assyria 'in my own land' (Isaiah 14:24–27), which readers connect with Sennacherib's retreat from Jerusalem in 701 BC (Isaiah 37:36–37). Sargon II, named only in Isaiah 20:1, takes Ashdod, and Isaiah walks barefoot to show that Egypt and Cush will be led off by the king of Assyria (Isaiah 20:4). Isaiah 19:23–25 then turns the enemy into a fellow worshiper: a highway runs from Egypt to Assyria, and the LORD calls Assyria 'the work of my hands'. Isaiah 23:13 points to Assyria's leveling of the land of the Chaldeans as a warning to Tyre.
sections.refs: Isaiah 14:24–27; Isaiah 20:1–6; Isaiah 19:23–25; Isaiah 23:13; Isaiah 10:5–19; Isaiah 37:36–37

sections.b: Isaiah 15–16 is the longest oracle on Moab in the Bible. It names town after town, Ar, Kir, Dibon, Nebo, Medeba, Heshbon, Elealeh, Jahaz, Zoar, as refugees flee south with what they can carry. The prophet himself weeps (Isaiah 15:5; Isaiah 16:9, 11). In the middle, Moab sends envoys and a lamb to Zion asking shelter (Isaiah 16:1–5), and the answer is a promise of a just throne 'in David's tent', but Moab's pride (Isaiah 16:6) closes the door. A prose note adds a new deadline of three years (Isaiah 16:13–14). Jeremiah 48 reuses much of the poem: Jeremiah 48:5 repeats Isaiah 15:5, and Jeremiah 48:29–38 follows Isaiah 16:6–12 closely. Whether the lament is sincere or ironic is debated.

common: Most readers take the prophet's tears for Moab as sincere grief, not mockery.
uncommon: Brian Jones and others read Isaiah 15–16 as an ironic mock lament that celebrates Moab's ruin.

sections.b: Isaiah 19 begins with the LORD riding a cloud into Egypt: its idols shake, its people turn on each other, its Nile dries up, and the famous sages of Zoan and Memphis give foolish advice. Isaiah 20 adds a sign-act: the prophet goes about stripped and barefoot to show that Egypt and Cush, the powers Judah trusted, will be led away as captives. But Isaiah 19:16–25, in prose, turns from judgment to healing. Five towns speak Hebrew; an altar to the LORD stands in Egypt; Egypt cries out under oppressors and the LORD sends a savior, as he once did for Israel; and at last the LORD says, 'Blessed is my people Egypt.' Jewish settlers in Egypt, from Elephantine to Leontopolis, read these verses of themselves.

In Isaiah's day the kings of Cush (Nubia, in modern Sudan) ruled Egypt as its 25th Dynasty. Isaiah 18 describes their envoys arriving in papyrus boats, 'a nation stretched tall and polished smooth', a people feared far and wide. The LORD will wait quietly and then prune the nations like a vine; and at the end the same tall people will bring gifts to Mount Zion (Isaiah 18:7). Isaiah 20 warns that Cush, like Egypt, cannot save the coastland from Assyria: its people too will be led off barefoot. An inscription of Sargon II at Tang-i Var says the king of Cush handed over the rebel Iamani of Ashdod in chains. Tirhakah, a later king of Cush, marches against Sennacherib in Isaiah 37:9.
sections.refs: Isaiah 18:1–7; Isaiah 20:3–5; Isaiah 37:9; Isaiah 45:14; Psalm 68:31; Zephaniah 3:10

sections.b: Isaiah 17:1–6 announces that Damascus will become a pile of rubble, and that Ephraim, its ally in the war against Judah (Isaiah 7:1–9), will be stripped like a harvested field and a beaten olive tree, with only a few olives left at the top. The prophecy was fulfilled in large part when Tiglath-pileser III took Damascus in 732 BC, deported its people and killed King Rezin (2 Kings 16:9), and when Samaria fell ten years later. The oracle groups Aram and Israel together: both had trusted their alliance rather than the God who made them (Isaiah 17:7–11).

In the year King Ahaz died, Isaiah warned the Philistines not to rejoice that 'the stick that beat you' was broken: from the snake's root would come an adder, a flying burning serpent. Readers differ on who the broken stick is (an Assyrian king such as Tiglath-pileser III or Shalmaneser V, or Ahaz himself) and who the worse snake is (a later Assyrian king, or Hezekiah, who did strike Philistia, 2 Kings 18:8). The oracle answers Philistine envoys with a word about Zion: 'The LORD laid Zion's foundations.' In Isaiah 20 the Philistine city of Ashdod rebels and is taken by Sargon's field marshal, about 711 BC.

sections.h: Dumah: 'Watchman, how far gone is the night?'
sections.b: The two-verse oracle 'concerning Dumah' (Isaiah 21:11–12) hears a voice calling 'from Seir', Edom's mountain country, asking the watchman how much of the night is left. The Greek titles it 'Idumea', and many think 'Dumah' (silence) is a pun on Edom. The watchman's answer is open: morning comes, and night too; ask again. Later Jewish tradition used the name Edom for Rome, and the Jerusalem Talmud reads the question as Israel in exile asking when redemption will come. Isaiah's full oracle on Edom comes in Isaiah 34.

Genesis lists Kedar, Dumah and Tema among the sons of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13–15). Isaiah 21:13–17 addresses these Arabian peoples: the caravans of Dedan camp in the scrub, the people of Tema bring water and bread to refugees fleeing the sword, and within a year 'all of Kedar's glory will be finished'. Assyrian kings fought the Arab tribes repeatedly, and the Babylonian king Nabonidus later lived for years at Tema. The Kedarite archers were famous, and Isaiah 60:7 later pictures Kedar's flocks brought to Zion.

sections.h: The Medes and Elam in Isaiah 13 and 21
sections.b: Isaiah 13:17 names the Medes, a people of the Iranian plateau 'who count silver as nothing', as the army the LORD rouses against Babylon. Isaiah 21:2 calls, 'Up, Elam! Close in, Media!' In 539 BC Cyrus, a Persian who had taken over the Median kingdom and ruled Elam's old territory, captured Babylon, and Isaiah 44:28 and Isaiah 45:1 later name him. Some scholars note that Elam and the Medes were also enemies of Assyria in the 700s, and set these oracles earlier.
sections.refs: Isaiah 13:17–19; Isaiah 21:2; Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1; Jeremiah 51:11; Daniel 5:28

sections.b: The taunt over the king of Babylon says, 'How you have fallen from the heavens, Shining One, son of Dawn!' The 'Shining One' (Helel) planned to set his throne above the stars of God and make himself the Most High's equal, but he is thrust down to Sheol. The poem is addressed to a human king (Isaiah 14:4, 16), and it uses the language of Canaanite myth. From Tertullian and Origen on, many Christians read it also as the fall of Satan, whose pride made him the devil; Jerome's Latin lucifer, 'light-bearer', became his name in English through the KJV. Calvin and most modern scholars read the passage of the king alone. Others take a middle view: the king is the subject, and the poem shows the pattern of satanic pride.

common: Many Christians have read Isaiah 14:12–15 as describing the fall of Satan through pride, alongside Ezekiel 28.
uncommon: Some hold that Isaiah 14 speaks only of a human king, using myth as satire, a view taken by Calvin and by most modern scholars, though it is less common among Christian readers at large.

sections.b: Isaiah 14:12–15 is one of the passages Christian tradition joined to the idea of rebel angels. Origen read it as the fall of a being who had once been without sin, and Gregory the Great and Thomas Aquinas cited it on the pride of the first angel. The poem itself speaks of a king who wanted to climb 'higher than the stars of God' and sit on 'the Mount of Meeting', the assembly of heavenly beings, and who is cast down to the Pit. The image of a star falling from the sky reappears in Revelation 9:1 and Revelation 12:4, 9.
sections.refs: Isaiah 14:12–15; Isaiah 24:21–22; Revelation 9:1; Revelation 12:4; Revelation 12:9; Jude 1:6

sections.b: Isaiah 14 gives the Bible's most vivid picture of Sheol. The world of the dead stirs to meet the fallen king of Babylon; it wakes the shades (rephaim) and raises the dead kings from their thrones, who greet him: 'So you are as feeble as we are!' His bed is maggots and his covers worms. Kings of the nations lie in glory, each in his own tomb, but he is thrown out unburied. The scene is poetry and satire, not a map of the afterlife, but it shows how Israel pictured the dead: weak, shadowy and still ranked by their earthly honor.
sections.refs: Isaiah 14:9–20; Isaiah 26:14; Isaiah 26:19; Ezekiel 32:17–32; Job 26:5; Psalm 88:10–12

sections.b: The king of Babylon boasts, 'I will sit on the Mount of Meeting in the remote heights of Zaphon.' The phrase draws on the Canaanite picture of the gods' assembly on a sacred northern mountain (at Ugarit, Baal's mountain Zaphon, and the assembly of El). The Bible uses the same language for the LORD's holy mountain, Zion, 'the heights of Zaphon' (Psalm 48:2), and for the assembly of heavenly beings around God (Psalm 82:1; Psalm 89:5–7). The king wanted a seat in that council above all its members; he was thrown down instead.

sections.h: The day of the LORD against Babylon (Isaiah 13)
sections.b: Isaiah 13 applies 'the day of the LORD' to a foreign empire: 'Howl, for the day of the LORD is close! It comes like havoc from the Almighty.' The day brings panic like labor pains, cosmic darkness (sun, moon and stars fail), and the shaking of heaven and earth. Jesus uses the darkening of the sky in his teaching on the end (Matthew 24:29), and Revelation's sixth seal draws on the same images (Revelation 6:12–14). In Isaiah the day falls on a particular city, which shows how the prophets moved between a near historical judgment and the final day.
sections.refs: Isaiah 13:6–13; Isaiah 2:12–21; Joel 2:10; Joel 2:31; Matthew 24:29; Revelation 6:12–14

sections.b: Isaiah's collection ends with Tyre and Sidon, the trading cities of the Phoenician coast. The oracle calls on the 'ships of Tarshish' to howl, because their home port is gone, and mocks a city 'that handed out crowns, whose dealers were princes'. The LORD of Armies has planned its fall 'to drag through the dirt the pride of all splendor' (Isaiah 23:9). Yet the end is surprising: after seventy years Tyre will return to trade, singing like a forgotten prostitute, but her profits will be 'set apart as holy to the LORD' (Isaiah 23:15–18). Tyre was besieged by Assyria, then by Nebuchadnezzar for thirteen years, and at last taken by Alexander in 332 BC.

Isaiah 23:15 says Tyre will be forgotten 'for seventy years, as long as one king lives', then restored. This is the first use, in the Bible's order, of seventy years as a fixed span of judgment; Jeremiah later gives the same number for Babylon's rule (Jeremiah 25:11–12; Jeremiah 29:10). An inscription of Esarhaddon says Marduk had decreed seventy years of ruin for Babylon, then shortened it to eleven by turning the cuneiform numeral around. The number stood for a lifetime (Psalm 90:10) and for a full measure of divine anger.

sections.h: A standing stone for the LORD in Egypt (Isaiah 19:19)
sections.b: Deuteronomy 16:22 forbids setting up a standing stone, 'which the LORD your God hates'. Yet Isaiah 19:19 promises 'an altar in the heart of the land of Egypt, and a standing stone for the LORD beside its border', a sign and witness like the stones raised by Jacob and Joshua. The priest Onias IV appealed to this verse when he built a Jewish temple at Leontopolis in Egypt in the 100s BC. The verse shows that the prophets could use the old form of a memorial stone for worship of the LORD among the nations.

The oracles against the nations are mostly judgment, but they hold some of the Bible's most open words about foreign peoples. Foreigners will join Israel when the LORD brings it home (Isaiah 14:1). Moab's refugees ask shelter in Zion (Isaiah 16:3–5). The tall people of Cush bring gifts to Mount Zion (Isaiah 18:7). Egypt will speak Hebrew, build an altar to the LORD, and be healed, and the LORD will call Egypt 'my people' and Assyria 'the work of my hands' (Isaiah 19:18–25). Tyre's profits will feed those who serve the LORD (Isaiah 23:18).
sections.refs: Isaiah 14:1; Isaiah 16:3–5; Isaiah 18:7; Isaiah 19:18–25; Isaiah 23:18; Isaiah 2:2–4; Isaiah 56:3–8

sections.b: Isaiah 20 is aimed at Judah's politicians as much as at Egypt. When Ashdod rebelled about 713–711 BC and sought help from Egypt and Cush, Isaiah walked stripped and barefoot to show what would become of those allies, and the people of the coast would say, 'So this is what became of the people we looked to.' In Isaiah 22:8–11 Jerusalem, under threat, checks its weapons, repairs its wall and secures its water supply, 'but you never looked to the one who did all this'. Isaiah does not reject defense, but trust placed in allies or engineering instead of in God.

Isaiah 22 shows Jerusalem preparing for siege, probably in Hezekiah's reign: counting houses and pulling some down to strengthen the wall, and building a reservoir 'between the two walls' for the water of the Old Pool. Kings and Chronicles credit Hezekiah with the pool and the tunnel that brought water into the city (2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:30), and both the tunnel with its inscription and the 'Broad Wall' have been found. The same chapter names two of Hezekiah's officials: Shebna, 'who is over the palace', is to be removed, and Eliakim son of Hilkiah is to take his place (Isaiah 22:15–25). In 701 BC Eliakim holds that office and Shebna is secretary (Isaiah 36:3).
sections.refs: Isaiah 22:8–11; Isaiah 22:15–25; Isaiah 36:3; 2 Kings 18:18; 2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:2–5; 2 Chronicles 32:30

sections.b: Among the oracles against the nations stands one against Jerusalem itself, 'the Valley of Vision' (Isaiah 22:1–14). The city celebrates on its rooftops while the prophet weeps for 'my dear people'. Its officers ran and were captured; its leaders looked to the armory and the water supply but not to God. When the LORD called for mourning, they feasted: 'Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!' Placing Jerusalem among the nations makes the point that God's own city is judged by the same standard.

The Old Testament background of 'the keys' is Isaiah 22:22. The LORD removes Shebna, the steward 'who is over the palace', and gives his office to Eliakim: 'I will lay the key of David's house on his shoulder. When he opens, no one will shut; when he shuts, no one will open.' The steward controlled access to the king and governed the royal household. Revelation 3:7 applies the words to Christ, 'who holds the key of David', and many interpreters hear Isaiah behind Jesus' promise to Peter of 'the keys of the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 16:19). Catholic teaching draws on the steward's office in explaining Peter's authority; Protestant and Orthodox readers stress that the key of David belongs to Christ, and that the keys of Matthew 16 were given for preaching, forgiveness and discipline.

common: Most interpreters see Isaiah 22:22 as background to the keys of Matthew 16:19 as well as Revelation 3:7.
uncommon: Some Catholic writers argue that the steward's office in Isaiah 22 implies a succession of holders, applied to the papacy.

sections.b: Two passages in Isaiah's oracles turn on burial. The king of Babylon, who expected a royal tomb, is 'thrown out, away from your tomb, like a branch nobody wants' (Isaiah 14:19), the worst fate the ancient world could imagine; Sargon II, who died in battle in 705 BC and whose body was not recovered, is one proposed model. Shebna, the palace chief, is rebuked for cutting himself a grand tomb in the rock (Isaiah 22:16). A tomb inscription in Silwan, facing the City of David, names an official '...yahu, who is over the house', perhaps Shebna himself.

sections.h: The prophet who weeps for the nations
sections.b: Isaiah 15–16 is written as a funeral lament: shaved heads, sackcloth, howling on the rooftops. The prophet joins in: 'My heart cries out for Moab' (Isaiah 15:5), 'my stomach throbs over Moab like the strings of a harp' (Isaiah 16:11). In Isaiah 21:3–4 he is doubled over at the vision of Babylon's fall, and in Isaiah 22:4 he refuses comfort over 'my dear people' while Jerusalem parties. Jeremiah takes up these laments (Jeremiah 48; Jeremiah 9:1).
sections.refs: Isaiah 15:2–5; Isaiah 16:9–11; Isaiah 21:3–4; Isaiah 22:4; Isaiah 22:12; Jeremiah 48:31–36

sections.b: In the middle of the oracles against the nations, Zion is the fixed point. When envoys come from Philistia, the answer is that 'the LORD laid Zion's foundations, and the poor among his people will take shelter in her' (Isaiah 14:32). Moab is told to send its tribute lamb 'to the hill of Daughter Zion' (Isaiah 16:1). And the oracle on Cush ends with gifts brought 'to the place of the name of the LORD of Armies, Mount Zion' (Isaiah 18:7).

In Isaiah's oracles against the nations the word 'remnant' (she'ar) is used of foreign peoples too, usually to stress how small it will be. Babylon's name and remnant are wiped out (Isaiah 14:22); Philistia's remnant is slain (Isaiah 14:30); Moab's remnant will be 'small, tiny, without strength' (Isaiah 16:14); what is left of Aram will be like the glory of Israel (Isaiah 17:3); Kedar's archers will be few (Isaiah 21:17). Israel's own remnant, by contrast, is a sign of hope (Isaiah 10:20–22).
sections.refs: Isaiah 14:22; Isaiah 14:30; Isaiah 15:9; Isaiah 16:14; Isaiah 17:3–6; Isaiah 21:17; Isaiah 10:20–22

sections.b: Isaiah 19:20–22 tells Egypt's future in the words of Israel's past. The Egyptians 'cry to the LORD under the hand of oppressors', as Israel cried out in Egypt (Exodus 2:23; Exodus 3:9), and the LORD sends them a savior, as in the book of Judges. The LORD makes himself known to Egypt, as in the plague story ('Egypt will know that I am the LORD', Exodus 7:5), and he strikes Egypt, but this time he also heals. The exodus becomes a pattern for God's mercy on the nation that once enslaved Israel.

In Isaiah's lament for Moab, the people of Dibon climb 'to the temple, to the high places, to weep' (Isaiah 15:2), and Moab wears himself out praying 'on the high place' but 'will get nowhere' (Isaiah 16:12). The Mesha Stone, found at Dibon, records that King Mesha built a high place for his god Chemosh there. The oracle presents Moab's worship as sincere but useless, a contrast with the shelter offered on Zion (Isaiah 16:1–5).

sections.h: Idols in the oracles on the nations
sections.b: Isaiah's oracles show the gods of the nations failing their peoples. Egypt's 'worthless idols' shake when the LORD rides in on a cloud, and Egypt turns in vain to spirits and the dead (Isaiah 19:1–3). Babylon's idols lie 'smashed into the ground' (Isaiah 21:9). Israel too has turned to 'the altars that his hands built', the Asherah poles and incense altars, but on that day people will look to the one who made them (Isaiah 17:7–8).

Isaiah 17:12–14 compares invading nations to the sea: 'booming like the boom of the seas, ... crashing like the crash of mighty waters'. In the Bible the sea often stands for chaos that only God can tame (Psalm 46:2–3; Psalm 93:3–4). Here God simply scolds, and the waters flee like chaff before the wind; by morning they are gone. In Isaiah 23:4 'the sea' itself speaks, mourning the loss of Phoenicia's sailors.

Isaiah 13–23 gathers oracles headed 'the oracle concerning' Babylon, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, 'the wilderness of the sea', Dumah, Arabia, 'the Valley of Vision' (Jerusalem) and Tyre, with shorter pieces on Assyria, Philistia and Cush, and a prose story of Isaiah's barefoot sign (Isaiah 20). They are spoken to Judah about the nations: a warning not to trust allies or fear empires, and a claim that the LORD of Armies rules the whole earth. The section ends with startling hope for Egypt, Assyria and Tyre (Isaiah 19:18–25; Isaiah 23:17–18), and leads into the worldwide vision of Isaiah 24–27.

Isaiah 23 pictures Tyre's trade as prostitution: after seventy years she returns to the streets with her lyre, singing so that people will remember her, and 'sell herself to every kingdom of the world'. The image is commercial: profit-seeking without loyalty. Nahum 3:4 uses it of Nineveh and Revelation 17–18 of Babylon the Great, with whom the merchants of the earth grew rich. Isaiah adds an unexpected turn: her fee will be holy to the LORD.
